# Conservative random chemical reaction networks

`bigan-conservative-crn` · *Bigan, Steyaert & Douady, 2013*

## Introduction

Take ten made-up chemicals with no structure at all, just the names `A0` to
`A9`, and wire them together with reactions chosen at random. Most random
reaction networks built that way are physically impossible: they create or
destroy matter, or they let a reaction run uphill in energy as easily as
downhill, which would make a perpetual-motion machine. Erwan Bigan, Jean-Marc
Steyaert and Stéphane Douady (2013) built random networks that obey two basic
physical laws. Mass is conserved: every chemical has a positive mass, and every
reaction has the same total mass on both sides. And the network is
*thermodynamically consistent*: each chemical has an energy, and the speed of
every reverse reaction follows from the speed of the forward one and the energy
difference, so a closed system settles into proper chemical equilibrium.

Their question was what such a network does, without any design, when it is
fed. Earlier toy models of the chemistry of life had used random reaction
networks (they cite Kaneko and co-workers), and the authors wanted to extend
that approach to networks that conserve mass and allow any combination of
reactants and products. They found that when one chemical is pumped in from
outside, a large network of this kind nearly always turns it into one specific
other chemical, and that the same chemical comes out whichever one is fed in.
They call this a "directed transformation machine". In the second half of the
paper they read that product as the raw material of a cell membrane and build a
*proto-cell* model (a minimal, hypothetical precursor of a living cell) that
can grow steadily when enclosed in that membrane.

It is a simulation model: a recipe for random networks plus rate equations to
run them. Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe it in their chapter on bio-inspired
artificial chemistries, among network models (book §11.3.2), where they note
that "such a simple toy model shows the ability to perform functions usually
prescribed to very specially evolved networks". Its nearest neighbours in the
catalog are other random networks of unstructured species.
[Random catalytic reaction networks](random-catalytic-networks.md) draw random
catalytic couplings between species but have no masses or energies;
[Kauffman autocatalytic sets](kauffman-autocatalytic-sets.md) derive their
reactions from polymer sequences and ask whether self-sustaining catalytic
sets appear. [ToyChem](toychem.md), the section before this one in the book,
also cares about energies but computes them from molecular structure. What
sets this entry apart is that mass conservation and detailed balance are built
into the network, not checked afterwards.

## How it works

### Molecules, masses and energies

There are `N` chemicals (ten by default, as in the paper). They have no
internal structure. Each one carries two numbers:

- a **mass** `m_i`, a positive number. The masses are not chosen in advance:
  they come out of the network-building step below, as whatever numbers make
  every reaction balance.
- a **standard free energy of formation** `G_i`, drawn at random. Free energy
  (Gibbs free energy) measures how much a substance "wants" to react: a
  reaction whose products have lower total free energy than its reactants runs
  forward by itself. Energies are given in units of `RT`, the gas constant times
  the temperature, and drawn uniformly between 0 and 15. The authors chose the
  15 so that the largest energy change approaches that of ATP hydrolysis, the
  energy currency of cells.

### Reactions

Only three kinds of elementary step are allowed, each involving one or two
molecules:

```
association      Ai + Aj -> Ak
dissociation     Ak      -> Ai + Aj
transformation   Ai      -> Ak
```

Dissociation is simply association run backwards, so in practice there are
two kinds of reaction, each kept as a forward/reverse pair. The paper also
defines *exchange* reactions, `Ai + Aj -> Ak + Al`, but leaves them out of all
its results, on the grounds that an association followed by a dissociation does
the same job. Chemart leaves them out too.

### Building a conservative network

A network is **conservative** if some set of strictly positive masses makes
every reaction balance. Written with the *stoichiometric matrix* `S`, which has
one row per chemical and one column per reaction and records how many of each
chemical a reaction consumes (negative) or produces (positive), the condition is
that a vector `m` with every `m_i > 0` exists such that `mᵀS = 0`.

The network is built one reaction at a time. Every possible association and
transformation is listed, shuffled, and tried in turn. A candidate is kept if
the network stays conservative with it added. The paper does this check with
Schuster and Höfer's (1991) algorithm for conservation relations; Chemart asks
a linear-programming solver whether a mass vector with every entry at least 1
exists, which answers the same question.

Two things happen as reactions accumulate. First, once the network has a
handful more reactions than chemicals, only one mass vector is left (up to
scaling): the masses are now fixed. From then on a candidate reaction is
accepted only if it balances under those masses. Second, eventually no
remaining candidate balances, and the network has reached its **maximum
size**. Both Chemart and the paper stop there. The paper's 100 sample networks
reached maximum sizes between 17 and 96 reactions (counting each
forward/reverse pair once), 42 on average.

### Rates, and why the reverse rate is not free

Each reaction pair is pointed "downhill": the forward direction is the one in
which total free energy falls, by an amount `|ΔG|`. The forward rate constant
is drawn around a typical value, `10²` per second for one-molecule reactions
and `10⁴` per molar per second for two-molecule ones (the authors took these
from typical enzyme rates). The reverse constant is then not drawn at all:

```
k_reverse = k_forward × exp(-|ΔG| / RT)
```

This is **detailed balance**: at equilibrium every reaction runs forward and
backward at the same rate, which is what thermodynamics requires of a closed
system. It is the whole cost of thermodynamic consistency here: one
constraint between the two rates of each pair, not extra data.

Here are the first reactions of the default network (seed 1), with the masses
and energies Chemart generated for it:

```
A1 + A3 -> A5  [mass-action k=10000.0]
A5 -> A1 + A3  [mass-action k=5852.229125020699]
A2 + A5 -> A0  [mass-action k=10000.0]
A0 -> A2 + A5  [mass-action k=62.318124632246665]
```

```
masses     A0 7, A1 1, A2 5, A3 1, A4 7, A5 2, A6 14, A7 14, A8 4, A9 1
G/RT       A0 10.62, A1 4.62, A2 7.70, A3 3.91, A5 8.00, ...
```

Check the first pair. Mass: `A1 + A3` weighs 1 + 1 = 2, and `A5` weighs 2.
Energy: the reactants have 4.62 + 3.91 = 8.53, the product 8.00, so the
association is the downhill direction with `|ΔG|` ≈ 0.54. The forward constant
is exactly `10⁴` because the default spread of rates is zero, and the reverse
constant is `10⁴ × exp(-0.54)` ≈ 5,852. In the second pair, `A2 + A5` (mass
5 + 2 = 7) forms `A0` (mass 7) and falls by about 5.08, so the reverse is much
slower: `10⁴ × exp(-5.08)` ≈ 62.

### Kinetics and the reactor

The reactor is a set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs), the rate
equations `dA/dt = S f + f_nu`, where `A` is the vector of concentrations, `f`
the vector of reaction rates and `f_nu` a constant inflow of one chemical, the
**nutrient**. Two rate laws are offered:

- **mass-action**: the rate is `k` times the product of the reactant
  concentrations, as in a dilute solution.
- **saturating**: each concentration `[A]` is replaced by `[A] / (1 + [A]/K)`,
  which grows like `[A]` when `[A]` is small but levels off at `K`. The authors
  added it because cells are crowded, and crowding slows reactions; mass action
  holds only in dilute media. `K` (the *saturation concentration*) is 10⁻² M by
  default. The reverse constants are computed the same way as for mass action,
  but detailed balance at equilibrium is then no longer guaranteed (see
  Results).

Because the network is conservative, the total mass `Σ m_i [A_i]` can only
change through the inflow: it grows at exactly `m_nu × f_nu`. That makes it
easy to see where the injected matter goes.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). N abstract chemicals A_0..A_(N-1), each with a random Gibbs free energy of formation

**R — reactions** (*implicit* — computed by an algorithm from the molecules that meet; molecules per reaction: 1, 2). association A_i + A_j -&gt; A_k ; dissociation A_i -&gt; A_j + A_k ; transformation A_i -&gt; A_j ; each kept as a forward/reverse pair

Reactions are added one at a time at random, keeping the network conservative (a strictly positive mass vector m with m^T S = 0 exists), until no remaining reaction can be added.

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time).

*How the population is bounded:* external nutrient inflow drives the system out of equilibrium

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("bigan-conservative-crn", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
bigan-conservative-crn: 10 species, 46 reactions, status=complete
provides: energies, flow, initial-state, mass-conservation, rate-constants, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
extras: conservation, energies, reaction_pairs
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
A1 + A3 -> A5  [mass-action k=10000.0]
A5 -> A1 + A3  [mass-action k=5852.229125020699]
A2 + A5 -> A0  [mass-action k=10000.0]
A0 -> A2 + A5  [mass-action k=62.318124632246665]
A9 -> A1  [mass-action k=100.0]
A1 -> A9  [mass-action k=8.488690652415743]
2 A1 -> A5  [mass-action k=10000.0]
A5 -> 2 A1  [mass-action k=2865.976715541064]
… and 38 more
```

The default call above builds a maximum-sized network of ten chemicals with the
paper's rate values, mass-action kinetics, a nutrient inflow of 1 M/s into `A5`
and every concentration starting at 1 mM, which is the setting of the paper's
nutrient experiment except for the rate law (the paper's Figure 3 uses
saturating kinetics; pass `kinetics="saturating"`). The paper's own reference
network, with 74 reaction pairs, cannot be regenerated: it is one random draw,
and Chemart's random numbers differ.

What the generator returns:

- `net.reactions`: forward/reverse pairs, adjacent, and
  `net.extras["reaction_pairs"]` lists the index of each pair.
- `net.extras["conservation"][0]["vector"]`: the mass of each chemical, as
  integers when they are rational; `"unique"` says whether the network is past
  the point where only one mass vector is admissible (always true at maximum
  size).
- `net.extras["energies"]["formation_free_energy_RT"]`: each `G_i/RT`.
- `net.inflow`: the nutrient and its flux; `net.initial_state`: the starting
  concentrations.

Building one network takes a fraction of a second; 100 networks take about
five seconds.

### Running the network

Chemart builds the network but has no general ODE integrator, so the
experiments below use a short SciPy function that turns a network into its rate
equations:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
import chemart

def rate_equations(net):
    """dA/dt = S f + f_nu for mass-action or saturating rates."""
    ids, R, P = net.matrices()
    R, S = R.toarray(), (P - R).toarray()
    k = np.array([r.rate["k"] for r in net.reactions])
    K = np.array([r.rate.get("K", np.inf) for r in net.reactions])
    f_nu = np.array([(net.inflow or {}).get(s, 0.0) for s in ids])
    def rhs(t, x):
        x = np.maximum(x, 0.0)[:, None]
        return S @ (k * np.prod((x / (1 + x / K)) ** R, axis=0)) + f_nu
    return ids, rhs
```

### The directed transformation machine

Seed 2 gives a 63-pair network. Feed it `A5` at 1 M/s with saturating kinetics:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("bigan-conservative-crn", seed=2, kinetics="saturating")
ids, rhs = rate_equations(net)
x0 = [net.initial_state[s] for s in ids]
sol = solve_ivp(rhs, (0, 1000), x0, method="LSODA", rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-12,
                t_eval=[10, 100, 1000])
```

Concentrations (M) at t = 10, 100 and 1000 s:

```
A0   0.00808   0.00808   0.00808
A1  0.000127  0.000127  0.000127
A2        30       300     3e+03
A3  0.000199  0.000199  0.000199
A4   0.00136   0.00136   0.00136
A5  9.37e-05  9.37e-05  9.37e-05
A6  5.21e-06  5.21e-06  5.21e-06
A7  6.89e-05  6.89e-05  6.89e-05
A8  0.000607  0.000607  0.000607
A9  3.28e-07  3.28e-07  3.28e-07
```

Nine chemicals, including the nutrient itself, sit at constant values while
`A2` grows linearly at 3 M/s. That is all the injected matter: `A5` has mass 3
and `A2` has mass 1, so 1 M/s of `A5` carries 3 M/s of `A2`'s worth of mass.
`A2` is also the lowest-energy chemical of this network (`G/RT` = 0.37).
Changing `nutrient` to each of the ten chemicals in turn, the same network puts
100% of the incoming mass into `A2` every time (measured from the mass growth
rates after 10⁴ s).

With `kinetics="mass-action"` and everything else unchanged, nothing settles:
at t = 1000 s every concentration is still rising, with `A9` (mass 6) the
largest at 493 M, `A3` at 14.9 M and `A2` at 3.8 M.

### Equilibrium against density

Close the system with `nutrient=-1` and vary `initial_concentration` to change
the total amount of matter, the *density* `D = Σ m_i [A_i]`. Integrating seed 2
to t = 10⁵ s (rates below 10⁻¹¹ M/s by then) and reporting the chemical that
holds the largest share of the mass:

```
                 D = 0.0024   0.024     0.24      2.4       24
mass-action      A2 0.985     A2 0.945  A2 0.725  A3 0.537  A9 0.695
saturating       A2 0.988     A2 0.993  A2 0.999  A2 1.000  A2 1.000
```

At low density the two rate laws agree. As density grows, mass action spreads
the matter and changes its favourite, while under saturating kinetics all the
extra mass goes to `A2`, the same chemical the fed network makes.

### Other settings

- Small and large networks: over seeds 0–19 at the default nutrient and flux,
  saturating kinetics sent at least 99% of the incoming mass to a single
  chemical in 11 networks. Three of those eleven (seeds 6, 8, 19) piled it up
  as the nutrient `A5` itself. In the other nine the leading chemical took
  between 62% and 96%. The small seed-1 network (23 pairs) makes `A3`, `A6` or `A8`
  depending on which chemical is fed, while the 63- to 65-pair networks of
  seeds 2, 12 and 13 make one product whatever the nutrient.
- `max_reactions` stops building early, for networks below maximum size.
- `s` and `p` spread the rate constants and saturation concentrations over that
  many orders of magnitude; the paper reports the same qualitative behaviour
  for spreads over several orders of magnitude, and shows results for
  `s = p = 0`, the default.
- `N` up to 20; for `N` below 6 set `nutrient` too, since the default `A5` does
  not exist.
- Slow settings: integrating to 10⁴ s with a small flux (0.01 M/s) did not
  finish within two minutes for seed 1 with the solver settings above. At the
  default flux each run takes one to two seconds.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `N` | `int` | `10` | structural | number of chemical species (the paper uses 10, and 20 for checks) <br>`2` … `20` |
| `max_reactions` | `int` | `0` | structural | stop after this many direct reactions; 0 builds a maximum-sized network (17-96, mean 42 direct reactions for N = 10 in the paper) <br>≥ `0` |
| `kinetics` | `enum` | `mass-action` | kinetic | saturating kinetics f = k prod [A]/(1 + [A]/K) models molecular crowding <br>one of `mass-action`, `saturating` |
| `k_avg_mono` | `float` | `100.0` | kinetic | geometric mean of monomolecular forward constants (1/s): k = k_avg 10^U(-s/2, s/2) <br>≥ `0` |
| `k_avg_bi` | `float` | `10000.0` | kinetic | geometric mean of bimolecular forward constants (1/(M s)) <br>≥ `0` |
| `s` | `float` | `0.0` | kinetic | spread of forward rate constants, in orders of magnitude <br>≥ `0` |
| `K_avg` | `float` | `0.01` | kinetic | geometric mean saturation concentration (M) for saturating kinetics <br>≥ `0` |
| `p` | `float` | `0.0` | kinetic | spread of saturation concentrations, in orders of magnitude <br>≥ `0` |
| `G_max` | `float` | `15.0` | thermodynamic | formation free energies are drawn as G_i/RT ~ U(0, G_max) <br>≥ `0` |
| `nutrient` | `int` | `5` | population | index of the species receiving the external flux (the paper uses A5); -1 for a closed system <br>≥ `-1` |
| `nutrient_flux` | `float` | `1.0` | population | external nutrient flux f_nu (M/s) <br>≥ `0` |
| `initial_concentration` | `float` | `0.001` | population | initial concentration of every species (the paper uses 1 mM) <br>≥ `0` |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "4 decisions"

    - Topology follows sec. 2.1: exchange reactions are excluded, candidates are tried in random order, and a candidate is kept while a mass vector m &gt;= 1 with m^T S = 0 exists (checked by linear programming). Once that vector is unique, a candidate is kept iff it is orthogonal to it.
    - Kinetics follow sec. 2.2 with the paper's values: k_avg_mono = 1e2 /s, k_avg_bi = 1e4 /(M s), K_avg = 1e-2 M, G/RT ~ U(0, 15), s = p = 0. The forward direction is the one with decreasing free energy, and the reverse constant is k_forward exp(-|dG|/RT) with c0 = 1 M. The paper's printed reverse formulas for mixed molecularity differ only by the c0 factor, which is 1 here.
    - Forward/reverse reactions are adjacent, with their indices listed in extras.reaction_pairs. extras.energies holds G_i/RT, and extras.conservation holds the admissible mass vector (integers when rational).
    - The old density parameter is not part of the network (the paper sweeps initial density to compute equilibria) and is dropped. The nutrient flux is the network inflow.

## Results

The paper (Bigan, Steyaert and Douady 2013, presented at the Journées Ouvertes
Biologie Informatique Mathématiques (JOBIM) in Toulouse, and posted on arXiv) reports four findings, all
from networks with `N` = 10; similar behaviour was seen with `N` = 20.

**Network size.** Once a network has a handful more reactions than chemicals,
only one mass vector is admissible, and networks stop growing at a maximum size
of 17 to 96 reaction pairs, 42 on average, over 100 samples. Chemart's builder
gives 11 to 99, mean 38.5, over seeds 0–99. The test suite checks that every
generated network has a strictly positive mass vector balancing all reactions,
that it is unique at maximum size, and (loosely) that eight networks fall in
the paper's range; a further test checks that every forward reaction runs
downhill and that `k_forward / k_reverse = exp(|ΔG|/RT)` for every pair.

**Equilibrium depends on density; under saturation one chemical takes the
excess.** For a closed network the authors computed the equilibrium at
increasing densities (their Figure 2). At low density the two rate laws give
the same equilibrium. At higher density, with saturating kinetics, all the
extra mass goes into one chemical. They also note that mass-action kinetics
guarantees detailed balance at equilibrium, while with saturating kinetics it
fails once the equilibrium departs from the mass-action one: some reactions
are then balanced and others not. The seed-2 table above reproduces the
qualitative behaviour; the tests do not check it, since Chemart does not
integrate the network.

**Directed transformation under nutrient flux.** Feeding `A5` at 1 M/s into
their reference network with saturating kinetics (their Figure 3), all
chemicals except one, `A8`, reached constant non-zero concentrations, and all
injected mass went into `A8`, whose concentration grew linearly. Other
nutrients gave the same product, which the authors call "an intrinsic property
of the system". Sweeping the flux (their Figure 4, after 10 s of integration)
showed a threshold: below it the injected mass is spread among chemicals,
above it nearly all goes to one. At still higher fluxes the network's
transformation capacity saturates and the extra mass stays as nutrient. With
mass-action kinetics the threshold remains, but all concentrations rise with
flux and there is no saturated regime. Across "tens" of maximum-sized networks
they saw the same qualitative behaviour, with the product statistically a
heavier, lower-energy chemical. The Chemart runs above show the same pattern
on large networks. On smaller ones the product can depend on the nutrient, and
some networks at 1 M/s appear to be in the saturated regime, keeping the
nutrient. The paper suggests that the maximum size of its networks is
presumably what makes the behaviour so robust, and leaves networks below
maximum size to future work. None of this is checked by the tests.

**A proto-cell that grows.** In the paper's second half the preferred product
is assumed to self-assemble into a membrane, which grows as the product is
incorporated and dilutes the contents as the cell's volume grows, while the
nutrient diffuses in through the membrane. Over a broad range of membrane
parameters the model reaches steady growth, and the cell's contents stay close
to chemical equilibrium, so they depend only on how much matter flows in, not
on which nutrient it is: a form of homeostasis. The authors describe the result
as a "machine that densifies matter" and compare it to autopoietic systems and
random chemotons without an informational template. Chemart does not implement
the membrane or the growth-dilution equations; it supplies only the reaction
network with its nutrient inflow.

The book summarises these findings in §11.3.2 but reports no later work
building on the model.

A note on the book's account: it says the authors stop adding reactions once
only one mass vector is admissible. The paper says they continue until no
further reaction can be added, and Chemart follows the paper.
